lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the project grapefern through the Ophioglossaceae body plan: one fleshy frond divided into sterile trophophore and fertile sporophore, with large eusporangia, no annulus, and subterranean mycorrhizal gametophytes.

project_scope.selection_mode: Source Sceptridium biternatum reconciled to current Botrychium biternatum
project_scope.note: Current Kew treats Sceptridium as a synonym of Botrychium and accepts Botrychium biternatum. Preserve Sceptridium biternatum as source/search provenance.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Do not look for sori on the underside of a normal fern blade. Follow the single frond upward until it divides into a sterile leafy trophophore and a separate fertile sporophore.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Terrestrial ferns arising from a short underground stem with fleshy roots. Fronds are often thick/fleshy and usually one per season in the Botrychium-type project concept.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Fertile sporophore is separate from the sterile trophophore and bears large exposed sporangia on branched axes. Sporangia are eusporangiate, thick-walled and lack an annulus; each produces very many spores.
family_diagnostics.gametophyte: Subterranean, non-green and mycorrhizal rather than a typical flat green surface prothallus.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: One frond split into leafy trophophore + grape-cluster-like sporophore = project Ophioglossaceae/Botrychium.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole frond bifurcation → trophophore → sporophore → large annulus-free sporangia → Botrychium biternatum blade → Sceptridium taxonomy card → Joey Pteridaceae contrast
visual_lesson.intro: Grapeferns stop looking like ordinary ferns once you name the two halves of the frond: one half photosynthesizes and the other is a separate branched spore-bearing stalk.

steps.title: 1 · Split the frond into two jobs
steps.look_for: A common stalk dividing into a leafy sterile trophophore and a separate upright fertile sporophore.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the fastest Ophioglossaceae recognition pattern in the project.

steps.title: 2 · Read the trophophore
steps.look_for: A fleshy 2–3-pinnate blade; in B. biternatum the terminal pinnae are elongated and nearly parallel-sided.
steps.why_it_matters: Gives the current project species a usable vegetative cue.

steps.title: 3 · Read the grape-like sporophore
steps.look_for: A long-stalked, branched fertile structure bearing many exposed globose sporangia.
steps.why_it_matters: Explains the common name grapefern and separates the fertile portion from ordinary sori.

steps.title: 4 · Show a eusporangium
steps.look_for: Large thick-walled sporangium with no annulus, producing thousands of spores.
steps.why_it_matters: This is fundamentally different from the small annulate sporangia of most familiar ferns.

steps.title: 5 · Teach the underground generation
steps.look_for: A subterranean non-green mycorrhizal gametophyte rather than a green surface prothallus.
steps.why_it_matters: Makes Ophioglossaceae's unusual biology memorable even when the structure cannot be seen in routine field ID.

steps.title: 6 · Update Sceptridium to Botrychium
steps.look_for: Source Sceptridium biternatum → current Kew Botrychium biternatum; Sceptridium retained as synonym provenance.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents a duplicate genus/species lesson and explains why older grapefern references use Sceptridium.

steps.title: 7 · Compare with Joey's Adiantum
steps.look_for: Joey's maidenhair fern bears spore-producing sori beneath a revolute blade margin; Botrychium instead sends up a completely separate branched sporophore.
steps.why_it_matters: A clean authoritative side-by-side of ordinary blade-borne fern reproduction versus Ophioglossaceae architecture.

comparisons.title: Ophioglossaceae vs Pteridaceae
comparisons.rule: Botrychium has a separate branched sporophore with large annulus-free sporangia; local Pteridaceae keeps many small annulate sporangia in sori on the blade, often under a false indusium.

comparisons.title: Ophioglossaceae vs Schizaeaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have visibly specialized fertile portions, but Schizaeaceae sporangia have a subapical annulus on modified frond parts; Ophioglossaceae has large eusporangia with no annulus on a distinct sporophore.

comparisons.title: Botrychium biternatum vs ordinary leafy fern
comparisons.rule: The grapefern's fertile branch is not an inflorescence and not a sorus-bearing leaflet—it is a dedicated sporophore arising from the same frond as the sterile trophophore.

visual_lesson.caveat: Older North American treatments often use Sceptridium for this grapefern group. Current Kew folds Sceptridium into Botrychium, so the learner keeps Sceptridium as searchable provenance rather than a separate current genus.

genera.fast_cue: fleshy frond split into sterile trophophore + branched grape-like sporophore

taxonomy_reconciliation.note: Current Kew treats Sceptridium as a synonym of Botrychium and accepts Botrychium biternatum.
Retain Sceptridium in search/synonym metadata because it remains common in field literature and project source data.
